Europe risks becoming a dumping ground for hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades but new research has found a ‘hot’ solution

Wind energy has been described as one of the “cheapest and most scalable solutions” to the climate crisis – but its boom is creating growing concern.

Turbines dotted across Europe and its waters are engineered to withstand some of the harshest conditions, from intense UV radiation to strong wind gusts, extreme temperatures and even lightning strikes.

While around 85 to 90 per cent of a wind turbine’s total mass can be recycled, the durability of the blades makes it difficult for the remaining elements to be reprocessed.

Wind turbine blades are clogging up Europe’s landfills

As a result, many turbine blades end up in landfill sites once they are decommissioned, typically after 20 years of service, or are incinerated.

Annual decommissioned blade waste in Europe is projected to increase from 20,000 tonnes in 2025 to 55,000 tonnes by 2030 as older fleets reach their end-of-life.

WindEurope, the European wind industry association, introduced a voluntary industry-wide landfill ban that came into effect last year to tackle this.

The association is urging EU policymakers to enshrine the ban into formal legislation, arguing it would further accelerate the development of sustainable recycling technologies.

Wind turbines undergo flash joule heating

Researchers have recently discovered a new way to give hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades a second life – by subjecting them to a “brief burst of intense heat”.

The study, published in the science journal Chem Circularity, found so-called ‘flash joule heating’ can transform blades – often made from silica-containing fiberglass and carbon-rich polymer resin – into silicon carbide and graphene, two valuable materials for manufacturing.

Blades were heated to about 2,000°C in seconds; at such high temperatures, carbon can react with silica to form silicon carbide, a hard, heat-resistant material.

Carbon can also reorganise into graphene under these conditions, a material known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity.

The research team found that adding the broken-down blades to other materials before heating made the new material more useful for creating new rotor blades.

Just 0.3 per cent (by weight) of the recovered materials was able to make resin stiffer and stronger and improve its resistance to deformation by 27 per cent under tension and nine per cent when bent.

“The mixture of silicon carbide and graphene can be incorporated back into resins for new wind turbine blades, improving their mechanical and thermal properties,” says senior author and chemical and environmental engineer Bing Deng of Tsinghua University, China.

“That is more than recycling – it’s upcycling. We’re turning something that has little value into something that’s worth much more.”

With airline alliances and partnerships, frequent flyers can rack up miles in their sleep.

Unless you’re an actual frequent flyer, you probably don’t pay much attention to loyalty programmes.

And why would you? You might assume that if you’re not constantly racking up air miles, it’s not worth your time.

That’s where you’d be wrong, because it takes very little effort to set yourself up in a way that will earn you points in your sleep, all of which puts money back in your pocket the next time you go to book a flight.

Here’s everything you need to know about the main frequent-flyer programmes in Europe.

Back to basics: Why should I join a frequent-flyer programme?

There are two main reasons to join a frequent-flyer programme: Earning miles, which can be used to pay for things, and earning elite status, which gives you benefits like lounge access every time you fly.

Confusingly, the names for miles and tier status points vary from airline to airline.

As an example, passengers flying with Qatar Airways earn both Avios and Qpoints with every flight. Avios can be used to pay for flights or upgrades, while Qpoints help you move between privilege club membership tiers.

The lowest tier on Qatar Airways is burgundy – to reach silver, you need to earn 150 Qpoints within any 12-month period. For gold, it’s 300; for platinum, it’s 600.

As a silver member, benefits include 15kg extra baggage allowance, priority boarding, and lounge access. You also get a 25% tier bonus on eligible flights, which makes it easier to keep the status once you’ve initially earned it.

As you move up the tiers, the benefits improve.

By contrast, the Air France-KLM travel currency is simply called “Miles”, while experience points (XP) help with your status tier.

The lowest tier is explorer; to become a silver member, you need to earn 100 XP in a year; for gold, 180 XP; for ultimate, you need 900 XP.

You earn more miles per flight depending on what tier you are (meaning you can save more money), while some tiers also have free seat selection, lounge access and additional baggage.

Which frequent-flyer programme should I join?

The short answer to this is: You should probably join all of them.

I’m certainly not saying pull up a list of every single airline out there and methodically make your way through them. But every time you fly with a new carrier, you might as well sign up while booking the flight, particularly now many airlines are offering free on-board wifi to members.

The long answer is: You should pick one main airline, then try to fly mostly with them along with other carriers that are part of the same alliance.

This is because you’ll be able to transfer miles earned between different airlines, meaning miles you earned flying around Europe with British Airways could be used to get money off a flight to Tokyo with Japan Airlines, or to Sydney with Qantas. All three carriers are part of the oneworld Alliance.

And why do airline alliances matter?

You could pick your main airline willy-nilly, but the easiest option will be to look at which airports are nearest to you and see if any of them are a home base for a full-service – not budget – carrier.

As an example, Amsterdam Schiphol is the home base for KLM. If you fly from this airport frequently, chances are you are already flying with them naturally as they will serve the most destinations from the Dutch capital.

By signing up to KLM’s Flying Blue frequent-flyer programme – which is also the same programme for Air France and Transavia – you’ll benefit from the SkyTeam airline alliance. This means you’ll be able to transfer points or miles gained from flying between carriers in the group.

In Europe, SkyTeam airlines include Air France, Air Europa, Scandinavian Airlines, TAROM and Virgin Atlantic, but the group also has carriers like Delta Air Lines and Aeroméxico in North America, plus Korean Air, China Airlines and Vietnam Airlines and Saudia in Asia.

If your nearest airport is Frankfurt or Munich, signing up for Lufthansa’s Miles & More scheme gives you access to the Star Alliance.

That alliance includes European carriers like Aegean Airlines, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, LOT Polish Airlines, TAP Air Portugal and Turkish Airlines, plus United Airlines, Air Canada and Copa Airlines in the Americas; Singapore Airlines, Air China, ANA and EVA Air in Asia; and Air New Zealand in Australasia.

Should your main airport be Madrid, then you’ll want to join the Iberia Club to access the oneworld Alliance.

European airlines signed up to the scheme include British Airways and Finnair; Asian carriers like Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Qatar Airways and Malaysia Airlines; plus Qantas in Australasia.

Budget airlines like Ryanair, Wizz Air or easyJet aren’t typically members of airline alliances, nor do they have frequent flyer programmes in the traditional sense.

However, easyJet now offers “easyJet Plus” membership, which is a set annual fee that gives benefits like speedy boarding, a large cabin bag included on board, and free premium seat selection. Wizz Air has a “Discount Club”, which includes discounts on fares and on luggage after paying the annual fee.

How to earn miles – without flying

The amount of miles you earn while flying depends on a number of factors, such as the seat class you flew in, your airline tier status, and either the length of the flight or its cost.

But it certainly isn’t the only way to earn – for many airlines, it’s not even how the majority of people do so. In 2015, American Airlines sold 58% of its miles to third parties, meaning just 42% were handed out through flight purchases.

Different airlines will have different partners, which you’ll be able to find on the relevant carrier’s website, but they typically cover travel-associated spending, like hotels, car rentals and tour operators. They may also cover retail brands.

Members of the Aer Lingus loyalty programme, AerClub, can earn Avios on Uber rides, by shopping at M&S, and ordering through Domino’s – you just need to make sure you’ve registered to collect Avios with the right partner.

Many hotel groups, such as Marriott Bonvoy or Accor, have partnerships with airline brands which mean points you earn during stays can be changed into miles, although the ratios may not necessarily be 1:1.

Throughout the year, hotels or airlines may run special promotions that increase the number of miles you earn for a set period of time.

While you may get an email about it in your inbox, you can also follow specialty blogs that are dedicated to maximising your loyalty points earning. These vary from country to country, but in the UK, there is Head for Points, while in Germany you can try Meilenjunkies.

These websites also go into detail about various co-branded credit or debit cards you can sign up for to earn miles, which I have not touched on at all in this article because I am not qualified to give financial advice.

All I can say is that it’s a big commitment, and that you should fully read all of the terms and conditions before signing up for anything.

Other ways to earn tier status

Another reason airport alliances matter is that some carriers offer status matches.

Essentially, this means that if you have reached the silver or gold tier with one brand, you might be able to get the same with another without having to match the number of flights taken.

Virgin Atlantic offers status matches for all the SkyTeam alliance airlines. For silver status, you need to book one Virgin Atlantic flight in any cabin and share proof of status; for gold, you’ll need to share the same proof but make a premium or upper class booking.

Outside of the alliance, Virgin Atlantic will also match status on British Airways, Iberia and Lufthansa.

How much are my miles worth, and what can I spend them on?

There’s no way to exchange airline miles for cash, so there’s no actual “worth” set in stone.

Points can be used to save money on flights, to pay for an upgrade, or to pay for the flight completely, although airlines will only have a set number of miles-only seats on each plane. You may also be able to use them at the airline partners where you can earn them, which we covered above.

When people talk about how much your airline miles are worth, this is how much money you are saving by using them divided by the number you have – so you may get more bang for your buck depending on what you use them for.

The blogs mentioned above will have various breakdowns for the different airline miles and recommendations for how to spend them, but of course, it’s up to you.

A few years back, I used my miles whenever I could to save money on flights, but nowadays, I prefer to save them up and upgrade to business class when I have enough.

Frequent-flyer programmes: The top tips to know

  • Pick a full-service airline that operates out of an airport near you, and sign up for the loyalty programme.
  • Take a look around your carrier’s website to check its partners – you might be able to earn points while shopping, eating out, or booking a hotel, not just while flying.
  • Find out what airline alliance they are in, and sign up for the loyalty programmes of other carriers you might fly with. Make sure you link your accounts.
  • Use your points to save money on tickets or to upgrade, or use them at other partners.

One of the UAE's most senior energy officials told Euronews diversification has carried the country's energy sector through months of regional crisis, as Europe looks to the Gulf for secure supply.

The UAE will remain a reliable energy supplier to Europe and the world despite the regional crisis, Undersecretary of Energy and Petroleum Affairs Sharif Al Olama told Euronews.

Speaking at ADIPEC in Abu Dhabi, Al Olama said the UAE's oil exports continued throughout the crisis and that the country is using the experience to strengthen its energy infrastructure.

"I'm glad to say that we have proven ourselves during this crisis," he said.

Away from the cameras, conversations among the senior officials gathered at ADIPEC from across the world were dominated by the threat of renewed military strikes in the region amid the ongoing US-Iran war. Many had resigned themselves to their inevitability, while still hoping diplomacy could find a way forward.

Al Olama was candid about the pressure the sector has faced. "This is not a big secret. We are going through a crisis. The first few months were very difficult."

He credited the UAE's long-term decision to spread its energy mix across nuclear, renewables and fossil fuels, with hydrogen and other future fuels in development.

"To diversify the energy sources was the right decision to make and it has helped in terms of making sure that our systems continue to operate and the services were uninterrupted during the entire period of the crisis," Al Olama said.

He credited investment in diversified export routes for keeping oil moving to international customers, with further improvement expected "as time goes by".

"In the case of our oil exports, it has continued during the crisis."

Lessons from the period are now being built into facility design, the capacity under construction and the back-up held across the system. "We have learned a lot from the current crisis when it comes to the design of our facilities, when it comes the capacities that we are building, when it come to the redundancy in the systems itself."

On renewables, Al Olama said the UAE now has around 8.2 gigawatts of solar capacity, with plans to grow to 20 gigawatts and beyond.

"We are getting some of the cheapest kilowatt-hours that renewable energies can produce in the world here in the UAE and we're only expanding on that," he explained.

"So there are massive projects coming on their way over the next few years."

Planning for AI demand

The rapid growth of AI data centres, a recurring theme on the exhibition floor at ADIPEC, presents what he described as a global challenge for energy planners, and one Europe faces as it races to build its own AI capacity.

"The growth you're seeing is no longer even exponential. It's a vertical growth. That's massive," Al Olama said.

The UAE's answer starts with efficiency, he pointed out, citing cases where AI tools have cut power consumption at some data centres by 40%. Planning for expansion, cooling and the use of existing infrastructure follows.

"This is a challenge that we're living through, but we are planning properly for the future," Al Olama said.

Asked whether Europe could learn from the UAE, he framed it as a two-way exchange. "I think, to be honest, it's not about teaching, I think how governments interact. We learn from each other."

He said the UAE is looking at rating data centres for energy efficiency and climate neutrality, and is sharing practice with European governments. "I'm 100% sure there are excellent practices in Europe that we are actually exchanging views on with our counterparts in other governments."

Al Olama's message to Europe and the wider world was one of reliability and partnership, with the UAE committed to its energy transition.

"The UAE has and will remain a very reliable energy supplier," he said. "We believe in partnerships, in successful strategic partnerships that add value both at both ends."

The UAE plans to bring a series of large solar projects online over the next few years as it works towards net zero by 2050, the same deadline the EU has set for its own climate neutrality.

To retire on 70% of their pay, workers on average wages could need to save more than €1,000 extra a month in Switzerland and more than €600 in Germany. Euronews Business compares the estimates for women and men across Europe.

Mandatory pensions are projected to fall short of the OECD’s retirement income target in 22 of the 30 European countries it studied.

In its Pensions Outlook 2026, the OECD estimates how much extra employees on average wages would need to save over a full career to retire on 70% of their gross pay.

Lithuania has the biggest gap as a share of earnings, at 20.7%, while Switzerland has the highest estimated monthly contribution, at more than €1,000 a month for men on average wages.

The OECD calls this the contribution gap. It is the extra share of earnings employees would need to put into a voluntary pension plan, on top of their mandatory contributions, to reach the target.

How much income people need in retirement depends partly on what they expect to spend. “There is no universal retirement income objective. Instead of using target replacement rates, one could use consumption benchmarks, which are target expenditure levels to reach specific lifestyles in retirement,” Stéphanie Payet, a policy analyst at the OECD, told Euronews Business.

The OECD calculates the contribution gaps, which vary from 0.4% in Turkey to 20.7% in Lithuania among male employees with average earnings. The rates are mostly the same for women. But in Poland and Hungary, the gap for women is 8.6 and 2.9 percentage points higher, respectively.

The gap is in double digits in many countries: Ireland (19.4%), Poland (17.3%), Croatia (15.7%), Slovenia (12.5%), Latvia (12.3%), Estonia (12.2%), Switzerland (12.1%), Germany (11.1%), Belgium (10.7%) and Iceland (10%).

“Where gaps are large, this means that people are often under-saved, and so they won’t have enough to have a good standard of living in retirement,” Professor Iain Clacher of the University of Leeds told Euronews Business.

Among other major economies, the gap is 9.1% in the UK and 6.2% in France.

It is smaller in Bulgaria (4.4%), Slovakia (3.9%) and Sweden (2.2%). Turkey has the smallest positive gap, at 0.4%.

In Austria, Denmark, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain, mandatory pensions are expected to meet the OECD’s retirement income target for men on average wages.

How much extra would workers need to save each month?

Euronews Business applied the OECD’s contribution rates to average gross wages in 2025. The same percentage can translate into very different amounts depending on what workers earn.

At 2025 average gross wages, the estimated extra contribution for men ranges from about €5 a month in Turkey to €1,084 in Switzerland.

The figure exceeds €500 a month in Ireland (€974), Iceland (€716), Germany (€617), Belgium (€556) and Norway (€532).

In the UK, a man on the average wage would need to save about €494 a month to reach the OECD benchmark. The figure is €238 in France, €64 in Slovakia, €68 in Bulgaria, €91 in Sweden, €111 in Romania, €129 in Hungary and €360 in Poland.

Even a relatively small monthly contribution can be a burden where wages are lower. Average gross monthly earnings in 2025 ranged from €1,549 in Turkey to €8,957 in Switzerland. They were €5,558 in Germany, €5,445 in the UK, €4,195 in Sweden, €3,830 in France, €2,078 in Poland and €1,772 in Hungary.

At those wage levels, a retirement income equal to 70% of earnings would be about €1,084 a month in Turkey and €6,270 in Switzerland.

Why do contribution gaps differ?

Payet said the differences are directly linked to how much income employees can expect from mandatory pensions. The replacement rate measures pension income as a share of a worker’s earnings before retirement.

“A lower replacement rate from the mandatory pension system means that you will need to contribute more on a voluntary basis to reach the target replacement rate,” she said.

Professor Traute Meyer of the University of Southampton linked Poland’s large pension contribution gap to state pension cuts after the transition from state socialism to a market economy. She linked Ireland’s large gap to the country’s traditionally low mandatory pensions as a liberal welfare state. She pointed to Sweden’s strong public pension mandates, rooted in social democratic governance, as a reason for its smaller gap.

“Low gaps may also mean only formal workers are protected, leaving many outside mandatory coverage (Turkey),” she said.

Purchasing power of money in retirement

Professor Lauri Leppik of Tallinn University said a small contribution gap tells us little about what a mandatory pension can buy in countries such as Turkey.

Clacher added that “The contribution gap alone does not give a clear picture as the other factor that is important is the purchasing power of money in retirement".

Pension income varies widely across Europe. In 2023, EU spending on old-age pensions averaged about €1,440 a month per beneficiary, according to Eurostat.

That figure covers people already receiving a pension, including those with shorter careers. The OECD benchmark is for employees entering the labour market who go on to complete a full career.

Retirement poverty

Meyer pointed to the risk of poverty in retirement.

“Research consistently shows that voluntary retirement saving is insufficient, especially among lower earners. People underestimate future needs, prioritise current demands, distrust private schemes or lack the means to save,” she told Euronews Business.

What could change before workers retire?

The contribution gap is a forward-looking measure. It does not tell us anything about current pensioners. “It is based on expected replacement rates for workers entering the labour force today, assuming the rules of the pension system will remain the same until these workers retire,” Payet said.

The projections include changes already written into law, including scheduled increases in retirement ages. Professor Marek Góra of the Warsaw School of Economics said further changes could affect how much workers need to save. In his view, higher retirement ages would reduce the need for extra savings, while lower replacement rates would increase it.

“As a result, the actual need for voluntary additional retirement savings is less clear-cut than the estimates suggest,” he said.

How does the contribution gap work?

Payet gave the example of an average earner whose mandatory pension is expected to replace 50% of their earnings. Under the assumptions in her example, putting about 9% of earnings into a defined contribution pension plan from age 22 until retirement would cover the remaining 20 percentage points.

Take a worker earning €3,000 a month just before retirement. The 70% target would give them a gross retirement income of €2,100 a month. If their mandatory pension paid €1,500 a month, the shortfall would be €600 a month.

At a wage of €3,000, a 9% contribution comes to €270 a month. The worker would save the same share of earnings throughout their career, so the amount in euros would be lower when they earned less. Under the assumptions in the example, those contributions and their investment returns would provide the extra €600 a month in retirement.
